entry.title: Building the Company Dashboard: Managing Jobs and Applicants in ITConnect
entry.summary:
In ITConnect, companies aren’t just passive observers — they actively post jobs and look for talent. To support their workflow, we built a dedicated Company Dashboard designed for simplicity, control, and speed. Here’s what we focused on during its development: Key Features of the Company Dashboard Add New Job Postings
Manage Existing Jobs
View Applicants for Each Job
Technical Implementation Built with PHP and MySQL
Each job is tied to a company’s unique ID in the database
Secure job posting forms with input validation
Session-based access control to ensure companies see only their own data
Lessons Learned Structuring database relationships is key for efficient application tracking
CV files must be easy to access, but protected from unauthorized viewing
Keeping the interface simple helps employers stay focused on recruitment
The Company Dashboard is designed to be more than just a feature — it’s a daily workspace for companies hiring in tech. We're actively improving it to support more complex needs as the platform evolves.

entry.title: Building the Worker Dashboard: Managing Profiles and Opportunities in ITConnect
entry.summary:
At ITConnect, job seekers are at the heart of the platform. Our goal has always been to give them a clear, functional space where they can manage their profile, apply for jobs, and grow professionally — all from one place. That’s why we built the Worker Dashboard, a secure and focused panel for users with the “worker” role. What Users Can Do in the Dashboard Upload Their CV
Add Education and Background Info
Apply for Jobs
Role-Based Access Control
Technical Stack Behind It PHP + MySQL – backend logic and data storage
Session handling – to identify logged-in users and enforce access rules
Form validation & file upload security – for safe input handling
HTML + CSS – for a clean, accessible user interface
Key Lessons Learned CV Uploading: Requires strong validation (file size, format, naming)
Application Logic: Needs checks to avoid duplicates or spam
Access Control: Must be enforced at both front-end and back-end levels
The worker dashboard is more than just a user panel — it’s a personalized space where real opportunities begin. We’re continuing to improve the experience based on user feedback and usage data.

entry.summary: Falling Into the CSS Rabbit Hole (Yes Again), Cleaning Up EC Links, and Planning Visual Improvements Today didn’t go quite as planned, but I still managed to check off a few important tasks. Yet Again, Stuck in CSS Tweaks Most of my time was unsurprisingly eaten up by CSS. I got caught up in adjusting the finer details of the design and before I knew it, hours had passed. It’s still a work in progress, but I’ve started creating a more consistent and intuitive user flow. Better structure means less confusion for the user, and that’s a win. I’ll be experimenting with placement using the Z-pattern layout, which helps guide the viewer’s attention more naturally across the page. In Summary It wasn’t the most productive day in terms of raw output, but I did a lot of thinking and groundwork. Progress is progress—even when it feels slow. If you’re in the middle of building something too, hang in there. It’s all part of the process. Date: June 17, 2025 tags: portfolio, webdev, copywriting, ux, learning

entry.title: Smart Filtering by Programming Language and Location: Simplifying Search on Our Platform
entry.summary:
In platforms that connect IT professionals with opportunities, search is more than a feature — it's a core experience. Whether someone is hiring or looking for a job, finding the right match efficiently makes a huge difference. To support that, we built a simple but effective filtering system based on two key criteria: How Our Filtering Works Programming Language (e.g., PHP, JavaScript, Python, etc.)
Location (e.g., Tirana, Prishtina, or Remote)
The filtering is built using standard HTML forms that trigger PHP queries to our MySQL database. When a filter is selected, the system returns real-time results that match the selected criteria — keeping the experience smooth and responsive. Why We Focused on Just Two Filters (For Now) Programming Language reveals a developer’s core skillset
Location determines collaboration possibilities — local or remote
These two filters allow users to narrow down results meaningfully without overcomplicating the interface. What’s Coming Next? Level of experience
Availability (full-time, part-time, freelance)
Frameworks and tools (e.g., Laravel, Node.js)
Internship and freelance opportunities
These future additions will offer users more control and personalization during their search. Building this functionality taught us that simplicity is often more powerful than complexity — especially in early-stage platforms where clarity and usability are everything.

entry.title: Designing the Homepage & Hero Section: Crafting First Impressions
entry.summary:
After completing the core structure of our platform — from profile logic to backend APIs — we turned our attention to something just as important: the homepage. This is the first thing users see, so our focus was on making it welcoming, clear, and functional from the first second. The Hero Section — Clear Purpose, Instant Access The answer led us to a layout that includes: A search bar with tag-based filters
Real-time search results connected to our backend
Role-aware behavior — companies see worker results, individuals see jobs or freelance projects
This helps both user types get started right away without needing to explore the whole site. Testimonials for Trust Students who found jobs through our platform
Companies that hired through our network
Trust is earned, and showing real feedback early helps users feel part of a larger, active community. Simple Registration Cards "I am a Company" → leads to employer registration "I am a Worker" → leads to job seeker sign-up This visual and functional separation supports the dual nature of our platform and makes onboarding easier. What We Learned ? Designing a homepage isn’t just about visuals — it’s about clarity, simplicity, and removing barriers to action. Every section we added had to serve a purpose, especially for new users landing on the site for the first time.

entry.title: What Is the Walrus Operator (:=) in Python and Why It's So Useful
entry.summary:
Back in Python 3.8, a new syntax quietly showed up and turned out to be surprisingly handy. It’s called the walrus operator (:=). In short: it lets you assign a value as part of an expression. “I want to save this value and use it right now — in one go.” Here’s an example: while (line := input(">>> ")) != "exit": print(f"You typed: {line}")
What’s happening here: You ask the user for input (input(...)) You store that in the variable line
Then immediately check if it’s "exit"
All in one concise line. line = input(...) and then if line != "exit" separately. Use it when: You want to assign and compare in the same line (e.g., in a while or if) You’re inside a loop or list comprehension You want to avoid repeating the same function call A word of caution: avoid overusing it. If it makes your code harder to read, it might not be worth the compactness. with open("example.txt") as file: while (line := file.readline()): print(line.strip())
This is a clean one-liner for looping through file lines without a separate assignment above the loop. The walrus operator might look unusual at first, but once you start using it in the right situations, it becomes a natural part of your coding toolkit. Try it in small places, and you may find it simplifies your logic and keeps your code more expressive.

entry.title: Designing Two Registration Experiences: One Platform, Two User Paths
entry.summary:
As our platform began to take shape, we reached one of the most important steps in the user journey: registration. Our goal was simple, but critical — make it easy for both job seekers and companies to sign up, while keeping their data structured and separate from the start. 👤 Job Seeker Registration Name, surname, city, email, and phone number
Birthdate and the position they're looking for
Past experience, skills, and a short personal description
CV upload to support their profile with documents
Each field is designed to offer just the right balance between detail and simplicity — enough to get them started, but not overwhelming. 🏢 Company Registration Official email and business name
Business number and domain
Company website
A short description of what the company does
The idea is to create a solid profile for employers who want to attract the right candidates and post relevant opportunities. 💡 Why Two Forms? Validate input and data types correctly
Route users to the correct dashboards after login
Keep the backend clean and organized based on user roles
This split in the registration logic also laid the groundwork for our role-based dashboards, which we’re actively developing. We’re continuing to build the features on top of this foundation — and we’re excited to share more as we go.

entry.title: From Setup to Role-Based Access: Structuring a Dual-Experience Platform
entry.summary:
After completing the design phase in Figma, we moved into development with a clear goal: to create a structured, role-based user experience from day one. One of the first technical challenges we tackled was building a login and registration system that could differentiate between two core user types: Companies looking to find talent
Job seekers looking for opportunities
🛠️ What We Focused On in the Early Setup Project structure – setting up a clean and scalable codebase
Authentication system – allowing users to register and log in securely
Role separation – directing users to the right experience based on their role
During registration, users choose their role. From there, they are routed to different dashboards: Companies are guided to a space where they can post jobs and browse candidates
Job seekers see listings and projects they can apply to
🧠 Why This Matters By planning this from the start, we made sure the logic behind our app grows with us as the platform evolves.

entry.summary:

We began by translating our interface from Figma into real, working code. But as anyone who has gone through this process knows, the transition from design to development comes with a whole new set of decisions and challenges. Week 1: Setting the Technical Foundation Creating the initial project layout
Designing the navigation, footer, and main page sections
Building a login system that supports two user types: companies and job seekers
Setting up a database with key tables (users, companies, jobs, projects...)
Implementing a file upload system for CVs and profile images
Our Team & Workflow Erzana – backend logic and database structure Sumea – frontend development, bringing the Figma design to life Isme – authentication and platform security We collaborate daily using: GitHub for version control
Discord for communication
phpMyAdmin for managing the database
Early Challenges & Lessons Learned Handling multiple user roles in a shared login system
Securing access to pages based on user type
Validating user input and profile data
Safely storing uploaded files
These problems helped us grow technically and work better as a team. What’s Coming Next? Building a company dashboard to manage job listings and applications
Creating a worker dashboard for profiles and CV management
Adding a section for freelance project applications

entry.title: From Figma to Development: The Challenge of Choosing the Right Technical Direction
entry.summary: After carefully completing our project design in Figma, we thought the hardest part was behind us. But as soon as it was time to turn the design into a working product, we faced an unexpected challenge: We weren’t sure which technical direction to take. Each of us had different ideas. Some preferred a simpler and more straightforward approach, while others suggested a more modern and flexible solution. We spent time discussing, weighing the pros and cons of each option. What we learned is that this phase of the project requires not just technical knowledge, but also teamwork, compromise, and a shared vision of what we’re trying to build. In the end, we made a decision that felt right for us—as a team and for the goals of the project. In the next post, we’ll share more about the implementation process and the lessons we learned along the way.
